questions.q: In createServer((req, res) => { … }), when does Node.js call the function, and what are req and res?
questions.explain: The function is the request handler. Node.js calls it for each request with a fresh req and res.
options: Once for every request; req is the request that arrived and res is the response you build
Once when the server starts; req is the port and res is the host name
Only for the first request; later requests reuse its answer
Once per client; req and res hold every request that client will send

questions.q: The lesson's examples call server.listen(0). What does port 0 mean?
questions.explain: Port 0 lets the system choose a free port, so a test never clashes with another program. Read the real port from server.address().port after the "listening" event.
options: "Any free port": the system picks one, and server.address().port tells you which
The server does not listen at all
Only requests from the same computer are accepted

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: This handler answers every path the same way, so /anything gets 200 too. The status, the header and the body are exactly what the handler set.

questions.q: A handler sets the status and headers but forgets to call res.end(). What happens?
questions.explain: Every request must end with exactly one res.end. Without it, the client waits until it gives up.
options: The response never finishes, so the client keeps waiting
Node.js sends an empty 200 response automatically

questions.q: What does the response header Content-Type: application/json do?
questions.explain: A header is information about the response. You still turn the object into text yourself with JSON.stringify.
options: It tells the client that the body is JSON text, so it knows how to read it
It turns the object you pass to res.end into JSON
It checks that the client sent valid JSON

questions.q: The client sends headers with capital letters. What does this print?
questions.explain: Header names arrive in lower case, whatever case the client used. So read req.headers["x-task-owner"]; the capitalised name is not there.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: req.url is the path and the query string, without the host. Comparing it with "/tasks" fails as soon as there is a query. Route on new URL(req.url, "http://localhost").pathname.

questions.q: Which is the right way to find the path to route on?
questions.explain: req.url includes the query string, so /tasks?done=true would not equal /tasks. URL needs a base because req.url is only the path; pathname is the path without the query.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A known path with the wrong method gets 405, with an Allow header listing the methods that would work. An unknown path gets 404. headers.get returns null for a header that was not sent.
options:
GET /tasks 200 null
DELETE /tasks 405 GET
GET /users 404 null

GET /tasks 200 null
DELETE /tasks 404 null
GET /users 404 null

GET /tasks 200 GET
DELETE /tasks 405 GET
GET /users 404 GET

GET /tasks 200 null
DELETE /tasks 405 GET
GET /users 405 GET

questions.q: Your server has only GET /tasks. A client sends PUT /tasks. Which status code fits best?
questions.explain: The path exists, but not with this method: that is 405. A path the server does not know at all is 404.
options: 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow: GET header

questions.q: Why does the lesson write a small sendJson(res, status, body) helper?
questions.explain: Repeating three lines in every route invites mistakes, such as a forgotten header. One helper keeps every answer consistent.
options: So every JSON answer sets its status, its Content-Type and its body the same way
Because res.end cannot send text without it
Because Node.js requires a function with that name
To make the server read request bodies faster

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The number of parts must match, and fixed parts must be equal. A parameter is always text ("42", not 42), and decodeURIComponent turns %2F into /: anything can arrive in a parameter.

questions.q: A route parameter id arrives from /tasks/42. Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Everything in a URL is text, and anybody can send anything, such as /tasks/abc or /tasks/-3. Validate the text, then convert it.
options: It is the text "42", input from a stranger, and must be checked before use
It is the number 42, because the path contains digits
It is always a valid id, because the route matched
It is undefined until the body is read

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pattern allows only a digit from 1 to 9 followed by up to eight more digits, with nothing before or after. Leading zeros, decimals and spaces are refused.

questions.q: Why does the lesson check the text with a pattern instead of just calling Number? What does this print?
questions.explain: Number turns empty text into 0, ignores spaces and accepts decimals. None of those is a valid id. Checking the text first is safer than converting and hoping.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: pathname has no query. Every query value is text, even "5", and a missing one is null. get returns the first value; getAll returns every value for a repeated name.

questions.q: A client asks for /tasks?done=false. What does this print?
questions.explain: done is the text "false", and any non-empty text is truthy, so Boolean(done) is true: the wrong filter. The build compares text with text: String(t.done) === done.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: URLSearchParams encodes values safely: a space becomes + and & becomes %26, so the & inside the title is not mistaken for the start of a new parameter. Reading it back decodes it.

questions.q: How does the body of a POST request reach your handler?
questions.explain: With no framework, nothing parses the body for you. Read it with for await (const chunk of req), join the chunks, then decode and parse.
options: req is a readable stream; the body arrives in chunks you collect
It is part of req.url after a #

questions.q: Why must a server limit the size of a request body?
questions.explain: An unlimited body is an easy attack. Count the bytes as they arrive and answer 413 as soon as the limit is passed, instead of reading everything first. Real JSON limits are often 100 KB to 1 MB, but never missing.
options: Without a limit, anyone can send gigabytes and fill the server's memory
Because JSON.parse only works on text shorter than 1 KB
Because Node.js rejects bodies over 1 KB on its own
A limit is only needed for file uploads, never for JSON

questions.q: This server reads a JSON body like the lesson's readJson. What does it print?
questions.explain: Plain text gets 415 (wrong Content-Type), broken JSON gets 400, a body over the limit gets 413, and the good one gets 200. Each problem has its own status code.

questions.q: Why does readJson join the chunks with Buffer.concat before calling toString("utf8")?
questions.explain: This is the café problem from Streams and buffers. req.setEncoding("utf8") is another correct way: the stream then decodes across chunks for you.
options: A character cut in half between two chunks is only decoded correctly once the bytes are joined
Because toString does not work on a single chunk
To make the body smaller before parsing

questions.q: JSON.parse fails on a request body. What should the server send back?
questions.explain: Broken input is the client's mistake, so 400. The message should be your own: error messages you did not write can reveal details about your code, so keep them on the server.
options: A 400 with a short message you wrote, such as {"error":"Body is not valid JSON"}
A 400 with the SyntaxError's message and stack trace, so the client can debug
A 500, because an exception was thrown
A 200 with an empty object, so the client does not see an error

questions.q: What does the first digit of a status code tell you?
questions.explain: Clients check the status code first. A 4xx means "fix your request"; a 5xx means "not your fault, the server broke".
options: 2xx success, 4xx the client made a mistake, 5xx the server failed
2xx the client made a mistake, 4xx success, 5xx a redirect
How many seconds the server took to answer
The version of HTTP that was used

questions.q: A logged-in user who is not an admin tries to delete another user's account. Which status fits?
questions.explain: 401 means "who are you? log in first". Here the server knows who the user is, and they may not do this: that is 403.

questions.q: A POST /tasks request created a new task. What is the usual answer?
questions.explain: 201 says a new record was made, and Location: /tasks/2 says where it lives. 204 means there is no body at all.
options: 201 Created, with a Location header pointing to the new task
204 No Content, with the new task in the body

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: STATUS_CODES from node:http holds the standard phrase for each code. 415 is about the type of the body; 413 is about its size.
options:
201 Created
204 No Content
405 Method Not Allowed
415 Unsupported Media Type

201 OK
204 No Content
405 Method Not Allowed
415 Unsupported Media Type

201 Created
204 Deleted
405 Not Found
415 Payload Too Large

201 Created
204 No Content
405 Forbidden
415 Unsupported Media Type

questions.q: When should your server answer 500 Internal Server Error?
questions.explain: 5xx means the server failed. Invalid JSON is 400, a missing task is 404, and a missing login is 401: those are all the client's side.
options: When something broke on the server that is not the client's fault, such as a bug or a failed database
When the client sends invalid JSON
When the requested task does not exist
When the client is not logged in

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The 201 answer carries the Location header and the new task. A 204 answer is finished with res.end() and nothing in it, so the body is the empty string.

questions.q: The build matches one task's path with a regular expression. What does this print?
questions.explain: match[1] is the text caught by the brackets. ^ and $ make the whole path match, so a trailing / fails, and the id must start with 1 to 9. A path that does not match falls through to 404.
options:
/tasks/2 2
/tasks/abc no match
/tasks/2/ no match
/tasks/0 no match

/tasks/2 /tasks/2
/tasks/abc no match
/tasks/2/ no match
/tasks/0 no match

questions.q: The build checks typeof body?.title !== "string" || body.title.trim() === "" || body.title.length > 200. Why the ?.?
questions.explain: JSON.parse("null") works and gives null. body?.title gives undefined instead of throwing, so the request gets a clean 400.
options: The body may be valid JSON but null, and null.title would throw

questions.q: Why does server.js start listening only when process.argv[1] === import.meta.filename?
questions.explain: process.argv[1] is the script Node.js was started with. When a test imports server.js, they differ, so the test can start its own copy on port 0.
options: So it listens on port 3000 when you run node server.js, but not when a test file imports it
So it only starts on Linux
So nobody can start the server twice on the same computer
It checks that the file was not changed since it was saved

questions.q: In curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Call Ada"}', what does -d do?
questions.explain: -i prints the status line and headers, -X sets the method, -H adds a header and -d sends a body.
options: It sends the text after it as the request body
It sets the method to DELETE

questions.q: The build keeps tasks in an array in memory. What happens to them when you stop the server?
questions.explain: Memory belongs to the running process. To keep data, you need a file or, better, a database.
options: They are gone; the next start begins with only the starting tasks
They are kept in the browser's cache
They stay in memory until the computer restarts

questions.q: Finish matchRoute(pattern, path). Split both on /. If they have a different number of parts, return null. A pattern part starting with : is a parameter: store the path part under that name. Any other part must be equal, or return null.
questions.explain: Compare the parts one by one. part.slice(1) removes the : to get the parameter name. The values stay text; the route handler validates them next.

questions.q: Finish parseId(text). Return the number when text is a whole number from 1 to 999999999 written with digits only and no leading zero; otherwise return null.
questions.explain: Check the text first with /^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$/, then convert. Converting first would turn "" into 0 and accept "4.5".

questions.q: The server knows GET /tasks, POST /tasks and GET /tasks/:id (id made of digits). Finish statusFor(method, url): return 200 for a known route, 405 for a known path with another method, and 404 for anything else. Route on the path, not on the query string.
questions.explain: Get the path with new URL(url, "http://localhost").pathname so the query does not get in the way. First decide whether the path is known, then whether the method fits: unknown path is 404, wrong method is 405.

questions.q: Finish readPaging(query). Read limit (default 10) and offset (default 0) from a query string with URLSearchParams. Both must be digits only, and limit must be from 1 to 50. On a problem, return { error: "bad paging" }.
questions.explain: A missing value is null, so ?? "10" gives the default. Check the text with a pattern, convert, then check the range. The maximum stops one request from asking for millions of rows.

questions.q: Finish validateTask(body) like the build. body is whatever JSON.parse returned, so it can be anything, even null. Return "ok" when body.title is a string that is not empty after trimming and has at most 200 characters; otherwise return "400".
questions.explain: body?.title copes with null. Then check the type first, so trim is only called on a string, and finish with the emptiness and length checks.

questions.q: Finish bodyStatus(contentType, text, limit). Return 415 when contentType does not start with application/json (it may be undefined), 413 when text.length is over limit, 400 when JSON.parse fails, and 200 otherwise. Check them in that order.
questions.explain: contentType?.startsWith(...) handles a missing header. The size check comes before parsing, so the server never parses a huge body, and a parse failure becomes 400.

questions.q: Finish kind(status). Return "success" for 2xx, "client error" for 4xx and "server error" for 5xx. Anything else is "other".
questions.explain: The first digit is the family: Math.floor(status / 100). That is the first thing a client looks at.
questions.expected:
201 success
204 success
404 client error
413 client error
500 server error
302 other
